data.title: A Fake Claude Install Guide on Google Is Deploying MacSync Stealer and Hijacking Crypto Wallet Apps on Mac
data.description:
A Fake Claude Install Guide on Google Is Deploying MacSync Stealer and Hijacking Crypto Wallet Apps on Mac

Mac users searching Google for help installing Claude Code are being targeted by a paid advertising campaign that routes them to a convincing but fake installation guide — one that tricks them into running a single Terminal command that initiates a six-stage malware chain, installs a persistent remote access trojan, captures screen content and ultimately replaces legitimate cryptocurrency wallet applications with phishing tools waiting for the user to enter their recovery phrase.

Key Points

  • The attack begins with a sponsored Google search result targeting terms like "how to install Claude on a Mac"
  • Victims are directed to a Claude.ai-hosted shared conversation styled as Apple Support guidance — giving the lure an appearance of legitimacy without being an official Anthropic page
  • A ClickFix prompt instructs the user to paste a curl command into Terminal, launching a six-stage infection chain
  • MacSync stealer collects browser credentials, Keychain secrets, Telegram sessions, SSH and cloud keys, screen recordings and cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases
  • A LaunchAgent persists a remote access trojan across reboots, giving attackers an interactive shell
  • Modified wallet applications — including hardware wallet companion software — display fake error pages requesting recovery phrases from users who open them after infection
  • Huntress analysts identified the campaign after responding to a customer incident in July

How the Attack Begins

Someone searching Google for Claude Code installation instructions clicks what appears to be a legitimate sponsored result. Instead of reaching official Anthropic documentation, they land on a page hosted on Claude.ai — a shared Claude conversation formatted to look like guidance from Apple Support.

The Claude.ai hosting is the critical element of the lure's credibility. The page is not an official installation guide, but it sits on a domain users associate with Anthropic's legitimate products, creating an appearance of authenticity that makes the social engineering significantly more effective than a generic third-party site would be.

The fake guide uses ClickFix — a social engineering technique that instructs the user to copy a provided command and paste it into Terminal themselves. The command is a curl instruction that downloads and executes the first stage of the infection chain. Because the user performs the execution step voluntarily, the action bypasses many security prompts and defences that would activate if the same process were initiated by an application without user consent.

The Six-Stage Infection Chain

The initial command launches a small zsh loader. Huntress researchers noted that the loader changes for each victim — a deliberate design choice that makes file-hash-based blocking unreliable as a defensive measure. The loader unpacks an encoded payload and initiates a six-stage chain that unfolds with minimal visible warning to the user.

MacSync then runs an AppleScript directly in memory — avoiding writing executable files to disk in a way that would be detectable through standard file monitoring — and requests a set of macOS permissions that include Full Disk Access. If the user approves, the stealer gains access to browser cookies, saved login credentials, Keychain secrets, account passwords, Telegram session files and cloud and SSH credentials.

A separate signed helper application requests Screen Recording permission, allowing attackers to capture the victim's display remotely once consent is granted. The signed status of the helper adds another layer of apparent legitimacy — a signed application is one that has passed Apple's notarisation process, which users are generally taught to treat as a trust signal.

A remote access trojan is installed alongside the stealer, persisting through future logins via a LaunchAgent — the macOS mechanism for running processes automatically at startup. This persistence gives operators an interactive shell into the compromised machine, the ability to execute commands and the capacity to transfer files in both directions indefinitely after the initial infection.

The Wallet Trojan Stage

The final and most financially damaging stage of the infection chain targets the cryptocurrency applications already installed on the victim's machine.

MacSync scans for dozens of wallet browser extensions and desktop wallet programmes, then copies and rewrites selected applications. Hardware wallet companion software is included in the targeting — the same category of application that the macOS malware campaign documented by SlowMist earlier this year also targeted through fake WKWebView interfaces.

Once the wallet applications have been replaced with modified versions, the attack enters a waiting phase. The attacker does not immediately attempt to steal funds — they wait for the victim to open one of the modified wallets themselves. When that happens, the trojanised application displays a fake error page requesting the user's recovery phrase.

The recovery phrase is the definitive credential for any wallet derived from it. Unlike a password, it cannot be changed after disclosure — it is the seed from which every private key in the wallet hierarchy is derived, and anyone who holds it has permanent, irrevocable access to every wallet created from that seed, regardless of what other security measures are in place. Once entered into the fake error page, the funds those wallets contain are effectively accessible to the attackers from that moment forward.

Why This Campaign Is Particularly Effective

Several elements of the campaign's design work together to defeat the defences most Mac users rely on.

Using Google paid advertising to reach victims means the initial contact happens through a channel users treat as trustworthy — a search engine result, not an unsolicited email or message. Hosting the lure on Claude.ai itself removes the visual cues that typically alert users to phishing — there is no suspicious domain, no obvious misspelling, no generic hosting provider.

The ClickFix delivery method means the malicious command is executed by the user rather than by a process that macOS security can flag as unauthorised. The per-victim loader variation defeats hash-based detection. The in-memory AppleScript execution limits disk-based detection signals. The signed helper application passes trust checks. The LaunchAgent persistence survives reboots. The wallet replacement waits quietly until the user opens the application themselves.

Each individual layer is a known technique. Their combination into a single coherent chain creates a campaign that is genuinely difficult to detect and interrupt at any single point.

What to Watch For — Defensive Signals

Huntress recommends that defenders shift from file-hash-based detection toward behavioural signals that remain consistent despite the per-victim loader variation. Key indicators include unusual curl activity following a Terminal launch, Base64-encoded content appearing in shell commands, unexpected downloads initiated from Terminal sessions and new LaunchAgent entries appearing after software installation activity.

Unexpected permission requests — particularly Full Disk Access and Screen Recording — should be treated as significant red flags when they appear following a Terminal command execution. Legitimate software installation does not routinely require either permission, and both are being requested as part of this infection chain to unlock MacSync's full credential and surveillance capabilities.

What Affected Users Should Do

For anyone who may have executed the lure, Huntress recommends acting immediately across several fronts. Disconnect the Mac from the network to interrupt the remote access trojan's ability to communicate with attacker infrastructure. Change all exposed passwords from a separate, clean device — not from the compromised machine where keyloggers or session theft tools may still be active.

Cryptocurrency assets held in any wallet that was installed on the affected machine should be moved to a new wallet generated from a completely new recovery phrase on a clean device. The trojanised wallet applications may already have delivered recovery phrases to the attackers, making any funds held in wallets derived from those phrases at immediate risk regardless of whether a fake error page was actually displayed.

Organisations investigating potential infections should examine browser sessions and cloud access tokens for unusual activity, review persistence entries beyond the visible installer, and treat the LaunchAgent as a possible ongoing access channel even after visible malware components have been removed. Removing the installer alone does not remove the attacker's access if the LaunchAgent and remote access trojan have already been established.

Sources

Huntress threat intelligence report on MacSync stealer and fake Claude installation guide campaign, shared with Cyber Security News, August 2026. Huntress blog post on MacSync campaign, huntress.com, 2026. Cyber Security News reporting on shared Claude chat feature abuse, macOS ClickFix attack tactics, Nova Stealer macOS risks and ClickFix Telepuz campaign, 2026. SlowMist macOS wallet trojan campaign reference, 2026.

data.title: Can the Crypto Industry Relearn Asset Creation Under the New SEC Rules?
data.description:
Author: Meng Yan


The SEC has just released a key proposal, Regulation Crypto Assets. This is not a statement of principles, but a complete set of specific rules attempting to answer the question: How should a crypto project legally raise funds, grow, and ultimately escape the scope of securities regulation from scratch?

... I quickly read through the datasheet on the SEC's website, summarized its main points, and commented as follows: The core of the proposal is two exemptions plus a safe harbor. First, a startup exemption, allowing a maximum of $5 million in financing within a four-year period. Second, a funding exemption, divided into two tiers: Tier 1, a maximum of $20 million within twelve months, and Tier 2, a maximum of $75 million within twelve months. Third, the investment contract safe harbor: once the project meets the conditions, the SEC determines that its tokens no longer constitute an investment contract, completely escaping the jurisdiction of securities laws. The design logic of the Startup Exemption is clear: to give project teams a regulatory buffer period to complete the development work promised in their white papers. The conditions include a four-year term, a one-time use, a $5 million cap, public disclosure of principles on the official website, and filing a Form NOR with the SEC. This path does not require financial statements, allows public offerings, and permits sales to retail investors; tokens are not subject to resale restrictions. Issuers can be individuals, teams, or even registered entities, which is quite favorable for early-stage development teams with limited resources. The Fundraising exemption references the framework of Regulation A but has been specifically adjusted. Issuers need to submit Form 1-CRYPTO to EDGAR, disclosing their financial status and financial statements; Tier 2 applicants require an audit. In return, they receive larger fundraising amounts and ongoing reporting obligations. The two exemptions are not mutually exclusive; projects can start with the startup exemption and then scale up using the fundraising exemption. The Safe Harbor is the endpoint of the entire system. Once a project completes or permanently abandons the core managerial efforts promised in its white paper and makes no further commitments, it can submit Form TR with an analysis. The SEC will then determine that the investment contract is null and void, and the token itself is no longer a security. The asset truly transforms from a fundraising target to a freely tradable commodity. This proposal deserves serious consideration because it needs to be viewed within a longer timeframe. After the FTX crash in 2022, the crypto industry essentially lost its ability to incubate high-quality new assets. Almost all of today's top-ranked assets were created before 2022. Regulatory uncertainty effectively closed the compliant fundraising path in the US, forcing new projects to either go overseas or simply abandon compliance altogether. If an asset market fails to create new assets for an extended period, existing assets will gradually lose their vitality. Liquidity will dry up, narratives will become outdated, and there will be no new targets for incremental funds. For a period after 2023, the crypto industry hoped to evade the challenge of creating new assets by adding new features to existing ones, but the bear market that has persisted since the end of 2025 has already refuted this. If the crypto industry itself cannot create new assets that are more attractive and dynamic than stocks, old-school crypto assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum will gradually decline. The Clarity Act delineates responsibilities at the market structure level, while the SEC's proposal provides specific pathways at the financing level. Both point to the same goal: to reopen the channel for incubating new assets from scratch. To add a more sobering context, the entire crypto industry is undergoing an unprecedented massive filter, with industry insiders widely expecting over 95% of projects to ultimately fail. Meanwhile, RWA has quietly become a major driver of on-chain transaction growth. Behind this data lies an uncomfortable truth: the industry is acknowledging that its ability to create native, high-quality assets has dried up, leading it to rely on leveraged off-markets based on traditional assets. This shouldn't be the fate of crypto. This positioning fails to leverage the technological and economic advantages that crypto and tokenomics should possess. Tokenization shouldn't just be adding an on-chain shell to real-world assets. The industry must regain its ability to create native assets; this is the truly noteworthy aspect of this proposal, as it at least reopens this door at the institutional level. If this path proves successful and the crypto industry regains its ability to create new assets, we can envision many new projects, including AI and robotics projects, launching via crypto. Under regulation, they can lay a solid foundation, create assets, and then scale up on platforms like Coinbase, Binance, and OKX once the basic quality of the assets is satisfactory. This would improve the overall standardization of the industry and reduce fraud, but it may not necessarily reduce speculation. IV. A Startup's Path Forecast Imagine a startup, Xyz, and see what paths it can take after its proposal is implemented. Phase Zero: The team first publishes a white paper-style disclosure of principles on the official website. This step must be completed before any token distribution.


Path 1, using the startup exemption. Submit Form NOR, committing to completing the promised development work within four years, with total funding not exceeding $5 million, including airdrops, staking rewards, and testing costs. No financial statements are required, public fundraising is allowed, tokens can be sold to retail investors, and there are no resale restrictions on the tokens. This path can only be used once, and Form TR must be submitted to close the deal after four years.


Path 2, using the fundraising exemption.

Path 2, using the fundraising exemption.

If Xyz needs larger-scale funding, or wants to skip the seed stage and directly pursue large-scale financing, it can submit Form 1-CRYPTO to access Tier 1 funding (US$20 million) or Tier 2 funding (US$75 million). Tier 2 funding requires audited financial statements, and a "test the waters" approach can be used before fundraising to gauge interest. These two paths can be used in combination: start with the startup exemption, and then scale up with the fundraising exemption once the product is viable. The ultimate goal is a safe harbor. Once Xyz has truly completed its promised development work, or voluntarily and permanently abandons its commitment to continue development, it should submit Form TR with an analysis. The SEC ruled that the investment contract was null and void, and the token became a regular non-security crypto asset, no longer requiring registration and continuous reporting. Secondary market trading was also exempted from registration requirements under state securities laws due to the definition of accredited buyers. V. Impact of the Clarity Act Finally, regarding the impact of the Clarity Act: The Clarity Act completed its procedural vote in early August, but the final floor vote was postponed to mid-September, and its passage remains uncertain. If Clarity is ultimately approved, it will establish a spot market regulatory framework for mature digital goods at the CFTC level, creating a division of labor with the SEC's proposal. The SEC's rules address the process of tokens going from zero to one, raising funds, and eventually losing their security attributes; Clarity addresses the issue of tokens circulating on regulated exchanges after they mature. The two are complementary rather than overlapping. If Clarity remains shelved, the project can still rely on the SEC's proposal to raise funds and enter a safe harbor, but the regulatory affiliation at the secondary market and exchange levels will remain in a gray area.

data.title: MANTRA Chain Freezes All Transactions After Attack As Developers Prepare Emergency Security Patch
data.description:
MANTRA Chain Halts After Upstream Software Vulnerability Is Exploited

MANTRA Chain has stopped its blockchain after an attacker exploited a vulnerability in an upstream software dependency, forcing validators offline and freezing transactions while developers work on a fix.

The Layer 1 network, which is designed for real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation, stopped producing blocks at about 11:13 pm UTC on Thursday.

The outage has also disrupted public endpoints, bridge operations and MANTRA-managed Inter-Blockchain Communication relays, preventing assets from moving across the network.

Upstream Vulnerability Forces MANTRA Network Offline

MANTRA confirmed the incident on 21 August, saying it had halted the chain as a precaution while investigating the problem.

The team said,

"We're aware of an incident affecting MANTRA Chain and have halted the chain as a precaution while we investigate. All endpoints and transactions are currently frozen."

An update on MANTRA's status page later said the attacker had exploited a vulnerability in an "upstream dependency", referring to software used by the blockchain but developed outside the network itself.

The team said it had identified the issue and was preparing a patched release, while validators remain offline as developers test the fix.

We're aware of an incident affecting MANTRA Chain and have halted the chain as a precaution while we investigate. All endpoints and transactions are currently frozen.

This means deposits and withdrawals to/from MANTRA Chain are temporarily affected. If you're unsure how this…

— MANTRA | The EVM L1 for RWAs (@MANTRA_Chain) August 21, 2026

Because validators process and verify transactions, restarting the network will require coordination across the validator set before normal operations can resume.

Deposits And Withdrawals Remain Suspended

The halt has extended beyond MANTRA's own infrastructure, with exchanges and ecosystem partners asked to pause transactions involving the MANTRA token.

Several platforms have suspended deposits and withdrawals, including Upbit, meaning users cannot move MANTRA assets on-chain while the network remains offline.

만트라(MANTRA) 거래 유의 종목 지정 안내

만트라(MANTRA/KRW, MANTRA/BTC, MANTRA/USDT)가 거래 유의 종목으로 지정되었으며, 이에 따라 입출금 서비스가 일시 중단됩니다.

MANTRA(MANTRA/KRW, MANTRA/BTC, MANTRA/USDT) have been flagged with investment warning, resulting in temporarily…

— Upbit Korea (@Official_Upbit) August 21, 2026

Trading on centralised exchanges can continue because their internal order matching does not depend on transactions being processed on MANTRA Chain.

However, users cannot transfer assets between the blockchain and exchanges until the network is restored.

The disruption has also affected bridges connecting MANTRA with other blockchains, adding further restrictions on asset transfers.

MANTRA Token Falls To Record Low As Trading Surges

The network shutdown was followed by heavy selling in MANTRA's native token.

MANTRA fell as much as 18.5% from its 24-hour high to a record low of $0.004126 around 11:00 pm UTC on Thursday.

It later recovered to about $0.0044, leaving the token down roughly 10% over 24 hours.

Trading volume surged nearly 600% to around $24 million as investors reacted to the network outage and uncertainty surrounding the incident.

MANTRA has not said whether the token's price decline was directly linked to the attack.

Has Any User Asset Been Compromised?

MANTRA has not disclosed which software was exploited or how the attack was carried out, and it has not confirmed that any assets were stolen.

The project has also not provided a timeline for restoring the network.

"We will not resume the network until we are confident it is safe to do so.”

The team added that it would provide regular updates as the investigation continues.

Engineering and security teams are working with external partners to test the patch and assess the network before validators are brought back online.

Users have been told not to take any action during the outage and warned about scammers offering fake "recovery" services.

MANTRA said users should not respond to people claiming they can recover assets or restore access while the investigation is ongoing.

MANTRA Chain remains halted.

The halt is deliberate. It freezes every transaction on the network, so nothing moves while we investigate.

We are not yet in a position to confirm scope or root cause. We can say that our investigations are yielding fruit.

Updates here on X every…

— MANTRA | The EVM L1 for RWAs (@MANTRA_Chain) August 21, 2026

The incident comes as MANTRA continues to recover from the collapse of its token in 2025 and subsequent restructuring and layoffs.

In June, the project announced that strategic backer Inveniam Capital Partners would acquire the platform, with the transaction expected to close in the third quarter of 2026.

data.title: OpenAI's Technical Error Locked Verified Cybersecurity Researchers Out of Daybreak — And the Timing Couldn't Be Worse
data.description:
OpenAI's Technical Error Locked Verified Cybersecurity Researchers Out of Daybreak — And the Timing Couldn't Be Worse

Several cybersecurity researchers reported on Wednesday that OpenAI had suddenly revoked their access to its Trusted Access for Cyber programme — a restricted platform that gives vetted security professionals access to advanced AI models with fewer guardrails than standard accounts. OpenAI confirmed the issue was caused by an error. The incident, which landed just days after the company launched its expanded Daybreak access tiers, has reignited frustration among the security research community about the reliability of AI access programmes at a moment when those programmes matter most.

Key Points

  • Multiple researchers on OpenAI's official support forums and on X reported having their access to the Trusted Access for Cyber programme revoked, with messages saying their identity could not be verified or their account was ineligible
  • Five professionals affected by the access revocations live outside the United States and Europe
  • One researcher said OpenAI sent an email saying their access to Daybreak Blue had been revoked "due to a technical issue affecting a limited number of users," with OpenAI stating "this was an issue on our end, and not the user experience we aim to provide"
  • Affected researchers are being asked to resubmit applications and complete the identity verification process again
  • The incident occurred just nine days after OpenAI launched the expanded Daybreak Blue and Daybreak Red access tiers on August 10
  • Beginning September 1, 2026, individual TAC members must enable Advanced Account Security with a hardware-backed passkey or lose access to frontier cyber models

What TAC and Daybreak Are

Trusted Access for Cyber is intended for professionals engaged in legitimate security research. Participants can use OpenAI's latest models to identify vulnerabilities, review software code, analyse malware, and report discovered issues to developers so they can release fixes.

OpenAI's own Trusted Access for Cyber page describes the approach as an identity and trust-based framework for putting enhanced cyber capabilities in the hands of the right users while still blocking malicious activity. Real security work often requires vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation — tasks that a regular chatbot may refuse because the safety system cannot determine whether a request is defensive or malicious.

Anthropic has a similar mechanism for vetted researchers: the Cyber Verification Program. Such programmes are intended to distinguish defensive cybersecurity work from potentially dangerous uses of AI tools.

OpenAI introduced Daybreak Blue on August 10 as an entry-level tier for most defensive cybersecurity professionals, providing access to general-purpose models including GPT-5.6 Sol with safeguards for permitted defensive tasks. At the same time, the company launched the higher Daybreak Red tier, designed for authorised vulnerability research, exploit validation and security testing.

How Verification Is Supposed to Work

TAC combines automated identity verification, including government ID checks and know-your-customer screening conducted through identity verification vendor Persona, with a tiered set of models purpose-built for defensive cybersecurity work.

GPT-5.6 Sol is OpenAI's most capable model to date for long-horizon cybersecurity work, including vulnerability research and exploit development.

On internal benchmarks the model scored 73.5% on ExploitBench 2 compared with 47.9% for its predecessor GPT-5.5, and nearly doubled peak pass rates on ExploitGym under time-constrained testing. OpenAI's GPT-5.6 system card classifies all three variants — Sol, Terra and Luna — as High capability in the cybersecurity category under the company's Preparedness Framework, one step below the Critical threshold.

What Researchers Experienced

The impact on affected researchers was abrupt and disorienting. Users reported that access had disappeared with no email, no warning and no notification. When they opened the cyber page, they saw the default verification page again as if they had never been verified.

At least one researcher successfully passed Trusted Access verification, received the "Welcome to OpenAI Daybreak Blue" email and had everything working fine in Codex — then literally one day later their access disappeared and Trusted Access suddenly said they were no longer verified. When they attempted to restart verification, their account showed as unverified and ineligible.

Some researchers who had been using the programme for months without issue were suddenly flagged. Support responses told them that OpenAI could not provide additional details about verification outcomes and that support could not override the result.

The geographic pattern added another layer of concern. Five of the professionals affected by the access revocations live outside the United States and Europe — a detail that aligns with the broader pattern of international researchers having more difficulty accessing American frontier AI tools for legitimate security work, a frustration that the Bitcoin Red Team campaign had already made visible when Rob Hamilton and others were forced to use Chinese open-source models after being blocked by American AI systems.

The Verification Complexity

The verification problems are not entirely new. At least one security researcher working for a major enterprise and already a member of Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program had attempted to apply for TAC as an individual and encountered a bug where Persona verification succeeded but the system continuously returned the message "your identity couldn't be verified."

OpenAI's own help documentation acknowledges that if verification fails, support cannot manually override a verification result or provide additional details about why a specific result occurred. At this time, Trusted Access for Cyber verification does not support retries or appeals. That policy — combined with the technical error that revoked previously approved access — left researchers in a position where they had no recourse beyond resubmitting their applications from scratch.

The Hardware Passkey Mandate Coming September 1

The access revocation incident arrives alongside a new security requirement that will add another layer of friction for TAC participants. Beginning September 1, 2026, individual members of OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber programme must enable Advanced Account Security with a hardware-backed passkey or lose access to frontier cyber models. Members who do not meet the requirement will still be able to use ChatGPT, but their accounts will return to the standard level of model access.

OpenAI does not require TAC members to purchase specific hardware keys — the Advanced Account Security page says users can enrol with any compatible FIDO security key. The verification process is conducted via Persona to help OpenAI determine whether an account belongs to a real user engaged in legitimate cybersecurity work.

The passkey mandate is a legitimate security improvement — hardware authentication significantly reduces the risk of account compromise that could expose restricted AI capabilities to unauthorised actors. But its introduction while the programme is simultaneously experiencing access revocation errors compounds the operational friction for the security researchers the programme is designed to serve.

Why the Timing Matters

The TAC access incident occurred amid wider criticism of OpenAI and Anthropic from cybersecurity researchers — criticism that has become substantially more pointed in recent weeks following the Bitcoin Red Team campaign's public documentation that American AI models were blocking legitimate defensive security work while Chinese open-source models delivered confirmed results.

The access revocation error, however unintentional, lands in that context in a way that reinforces the frustration. Researchers who completed identity verification, received welcome emails, used the programme successfully and then found their access silently revoked are not being served by the programme as designed. The inability of support to override verification results or explain what triggered the revocation adds opacity to a process that is already demanding significant personal information from researchers in exchange for access.

The balance is difficult. A regular chatbot can refuse many cybersecurity prompts because the safety system does not know whether a request is defensive or malicious. But real security work often requires vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation. OpenAI has been trying to solve that problem through Daybreak. A technical error that revokes verified access without notice — and without a functioning appeals process — is a reminder of how fragile that balance remains in practice.

Sources

TechCrunch reporting on OpenAI TAC access revocations, August 19, 2026. Mezha reporting on OpenAI technical error and Daybreak Blue revocations, August 2026. TechBooky analysis of OpenAI cyber access error implications, August 2026. Cloud Security Alliance research note on OpenAI hardware passkey mandate for TAC, 2026. Biometric Update reporting on OpenAI hardware-backed passkey requirement, July 2026. OpenAI Developer Community forum posts on TAC access disappearance, August 2026. OpenAI Help Center documentation on Trusted Access for Cyber common issues and troubleshooting.

data.title: Google To Refund Millions After $700 Million Settlement Over Google Play App And Payment Practices
data.description:
Google To Pay $700 Million Over Google Play Antitrust Claims

Google will pay $700 million to settle a five-year multistate antitrust case over how it operates the Google Play Store, after a federal court approved an agreement that will provide refunds to affected consumers across the US.

The lawsuit accused Google of using its control over Android app distribution and in-app payments to limit competition and charge consumers as much as 30% more on transactions made through Google Play.

Millions Of Consumers Set To Receive Refunds

A large share of the settlement will go to people who bought apps, games and other products through Google Play between August 2016 and September 2023.

Washington is expected to receive about $13 million, with around 2.4 million residents potentially eligible for payments.

When giant companies gain an illegal stranglehold on a market, we take action and deliver relief for consumers.

A federal court today approved a $700 million settlement in a multistate antitrust lawsuit against Google. The lawsuit challenged Google's control over Android app… pic.twitter.com/Yv1gsUVsTC

— Attorney General Nick Brown (@AGOWA) August 18, 2026

Most consumers who qualify will not need to file a claim.

Payments will generally be made through PayPal or Venmo, while people unable to use either service will have another way to submit a claim and receive their money.

Google Must Open Up Its Play Store Practices

The settlement also requires Google to make several changes to its business practices.

For at least five years, Android app developers will be allowed to use alternative payment systems and tell customers about potentially cheaper purchasing options outside Google's billing system.

Developers will also be able to distribute their apps through competing app stores without facing retaliation from Google.

Android users will have another route to apps as well, with the agreement requiring Google to allow app installations from sources outside the Google Play Store for at least seven years.

Washington Attorney General Says Consumers Will Get Relief

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown said the case was part of his office's efforts to challenge companies accused of using excessive market power.

“When giant companies gain an illegal stranglehold on a market, we take action and deliver relief for consumers. Fighting monopolies is one of our office’s core responsibilities, and I’m proud that millions of Washingtonians will now get refunds because of our litigation.”

Google has denied wrongdoing in the case, despite agreeing to the settlement and the changes to its Play Store practices.

data.title: Visa Seeks New Stablecoin Settlement Partner After Mastercard Completes $1.8 Billion BVNK Acquisition
data.description:
Visa Hunts For New Stablecoin Partner After Mastercard Acquires BVNK

Visa is looking for a new firm to handle stablecoin settlement and over-the-counter trading after Mastercard completed its acquisition of BVNK, the infrastructure provider that had previously worked with Visa.

The payments giant has issued a request for proposals seeking a partner that can support stablecoin swaps and settlement across major markets, with a particularly strict licensing requirement covering the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and Singapore.

LATEST: ⚡ Visa is looking for new stablecoin settlement partners after Mastercard acquired BVNK, seeking firms licensed in the US, UK, Canada and Singapore. pic.twitter.com/q36HI2d6Ta

— CoinMarketCap (@CoinMarketCap) August 19, 2026

Visa Needs A Partner With Licences In Four Markets

According to a request for proposals reported by CoinDesk, Visa is seeking both a settlement partner and an OTC partner capable of handling multiple stablecoins.

Each prospective partner must hold cryptocurrency exchange licences in all four required jurisdictions, limiting the number of firms that can qualify for the role.

Visa declined to comment on the reported documents.

The search follows Mastercard's completion of its BVNK acquisition on 3 August 2026.

Mastercard announced the deal on 17 March 2026 at a valuation of up to $1.8 billion, including $300 million in potential contingent payments.

BVNK had built infrastructure for fiat and on-chain payments across more than 130 countries, making its move to Mastercard particularly important for Visa as it develops its own stablecoin services.

Mastercard Closes $1.8B BVNK Deal To Expand Stablecoins

Mastercard has completed its $1.8 billion acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure firm BVNK.

The deal combines Mastercard's global payments network with BVNK's onchain technology. The companies aim to expand stablecoin… pic.twitter.com/rXcYpvGX2a

— BSCN (@BSCNews) August 4, 2026

How Mastercard Took BVNK Away From Visa

Visa and BVNK had previously worked closely together.

Visa took a strategic stake in BVNK in May 2025 at a valuation of roughly $750 million, before partnering with the company in January 2026 to support stablecoin payments through Visa Direct.

Mastercard's acquisition brought that independent relationship to an end and gave its rival control of BVNK's infrastructure.

Mastercard plans to integrate BVNK's technology into Mastercard Move, its cross-border and remittance network, to support stablecoin settlement around the clock.

The acquisition also came after a roughly $2 billion deal between BVNK and Coinbase collapsed late last year, leaving Mastercard as the eventual buyer.

Open USD Is Central To Visa's Search

Visa's new partner will also need to support Open USD, or OUSD, as the payments company expands its stablecoin settlement infrastructure.

Open USD is a multi-stablecoin project backed by more than 140 businesses, including Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, BlackRock, Google, Coinbase and DBS.

Open Standard launched the project on 30 June 2026, with OUSD expected to go live later this year.

Visa building Open USD and seeking a new stablecoin partner for 24/7 cross-border settlements is a logical expansion.

The push for faster, lower-cost international transfers continues to move traditional payment networks deeper into stablecoin infrastructure.

— Manan Sharma (@TraderXRahul) August 18, 2026

The project is designed to allow businesses to mint and redeem the token without fees or volume limits, while returning most reserve earnings to distribution partners.

Rather than relying on one stablecoin issuer, Open USD is intended to support multiple stablecoins, giving settlement infrastructure an important role in the project.

Visa's Chief Product and Strategy Officer Jack Forestell said on 30 June 2026:

"In payments, scale only comes with trust. As stablecoins evolve, the focus must shift from speed to reliability, governance and interoperability."

Visa Builds Its Own Stablecoin Platform

The search for a replacement partner comes as Visa expands its own stablecoin infrastructure.

Visa launched the Visa Stablecoin Platform on 16 July 2026, giving banks, fintech companies and payment providers tools to access, store, redeem and transfer stablecoins through a Visa-managed environment.

Good afternoon X Legends

⚙️ Visa’s latest stablecoin move is more interesting than another settlement announcement.

The Visa Stablecoin Platform is being built as an enterprise operating layer where institutions can mint, redeem, hold and transfer stablecoins from one managed… pic.twitter.com/5ZNmeoWYfW

— Crypto Poolz (@Crypto__Poolz) August 14, 2026

Open USD was the first token supported on the platform, linking the new system directly to the settlement arrangements Visa is now seeking to strengthen.

The platform initially opened for beta testing with selected clients ahead of a wider rollout.

Visa And Mastercard Are Building Competing Stablecoin Rails

Visa's search puts the two major payment networks on increasingly competitive paths as both build infrastructure for stablecoin payments.

Mastercard now controls BVNK and plans to use its technology across Mastercard Move, while Visa is developing its own platform and seeking licensed partners to manage the underlying settlement and OTC activity.

For Visa, finding a firm licensed across the US, Canada, UK and Singapore will be an important part of maintaining stablecoin settlement capabilities as Open USD and its wider platform move towards commercial use later in 2026.

data.title: CrowdStrike's Global CTO Is Leaving to Launch a $170 Million AI Cybersecurity Fund — And Investors Are Selling
data.description:
CrowdStrike's Global CTO Is Leaving to Launch a $170 Million AI Cybersecurity Fund — And Investors Are Selling

CrowdStrike Holdings suffered a more than 4% intraday share price drop on Thursday after the cybersecurity giant confirmed the departure of its Global Chief Technology Officer, Elia Zaitsev — a 13-year company veteran who is leaving to co-found a venture capital firm targeting AI and cybersecurity investments. The exit raises immediate questions about technical leadership continuity at one of the sector's most prominent companies, arriving just days before a closely watched earnings report.

Key Points

  • CrowdStrike shares fell as low as $194.01, down 3.8% from Wednesday's close, on news of Zaitsev's departure
  • Zaitsev is co-founding Cognition alongside Gur Talpaz and Tayler Sipperly — both former CrowdStrike corporate development executives — targeting $170 million in fund commitments
  • The fund will focus on agentic AI and cybersecurity, with seed investments averaging $6 million and Series A investments averaging $15 million
  • Cognition plans to make three to four concentrated investments per year
  • CrowdStrike has not named a successor for Zaitsev
  • The company is scheduled to report fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings on August 26, adding urgency to the leadership question
  • CrowdStrike shares remain up 71.1% year to date but sit approximately 14% below their 52-week high of $225.53

Who Is Leaving and Where They Are Going

Zaitsev spent 13 years at CrowdStrike, making him one of the company's longest-serving technical executives and a significant architect of its product direction during the period in which the company grew from an endpoint security specialist into a platform spanning cloud workload protection, identity security and AI-driven threat intelligence.

He is co-founding Cognition with Gur Talpaz and Tayler Sipperly, both of whom previously worked in corporate development at CrowdStrike before launching an early-stage fund called Brightmind. The trio's track record includes what Talpaz and Sipperly described as the largest Series A exit in cybersecurity history — SGNL, a company they entered at a $105 million valuation and exited at $740 million.

Cognition is targeting $170 million in commitments and plans to lead or co-lead seed and Series A rounds with average check sizes of $6 million at seed stage and $15 million at Series A. The fund expects to make three to four concentrated investments per year — a deliberately selective approach that prioritises depth of engagement over portfolio breadth.

"We have this new attack surface that's being brought on by AI and agents," Zaitsev said in an interview, articulating the thesis that is driving the new venture.

The AI Security Thesis Behind Cognition

The fund's investment focus reflects a thesis that has gained considerable traction across the cybersecurity investment community: agentic AI — AI systems that can take autonomous actions across enterprise environments — represents what the Cognition founders describe as a platform-reset moment for security.

The argument is that AI adoption in the enterprise is creating a category of security risk that existing tools, built for a threat landscape defined by human attackers and conventional malware, were not designed to address. AI agents browsing, transacting, accessing credentials and executing code autonomously introduce attack surfaces and trust relationships that endpoint detection and response tools, firewalls and identity management systems approach with frameworks that predate the risk they are now being asked to handle.

"AI security didn't exist five years ago," Talpaz said. "But as the adoption of AI dramatically ramps up in the enterprise, it requires a new set of tools."

Cognition's bet is that the founders' operational depth — Zaitsev's product architecture experience combined with Talpaz and Sipperly's corporate development track record — gives them a structural advantage in identifying and supporting early-stage companies building in that emerging category.

The Impact on CrowdStrike

The market's immediate reaction — a drop of more than 4% intraday on a stock that has gained 71% year to date — reflects the significance the investment community places on Zaitsev's role in CrowdStrike's technical direction.

The departure comes at a delicate moment. CrowdStrike has not yet named a successor, leaving the company's most senior technical leadership position vacant ahead of its fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings report on August 26. That combination — an unannounced succession plan and an imminent earnings event that will draw scrutiny — creates a window of uncertainty that investors are pricing in.

Counterbalancing the executive exit, CrowdStrike announced on Thursday morning that it had been named the strongest overall leader in the 2026 Frost Radar Cloud Workload Protection Platforms report for the fourth consecutive year. Frost & Sullivan highlighted the company's runtime protection capabilities and operational reach across multi-cloud and AI workloads — capabilities that Zaitsev helped develop during his tenure. The recognition underscores that while the departure is significant, the technical foundation he helped build remains intact.

Market analysts noted that while the news triggered immediate selling pressure, it does not fundamentally alter CrowdStrike's competitive position in endpoint security and cloud workload protection. The Falcon platform remains a market leader in its category, and the company has demonstrated an ability to retain top engineering talent and maintain product momentum through previous leadership transitions.

A Broader Pattern of Talent Migration

Zaitsev's departure is not an isolated event. The cybersecurity sector has seen a significant wave of senior talent moving toward AI-focused ventures over the past year, as investors pour capital into startups addressing what industry leaders broadly describe as an expanding threat landscape driven by autonomous agents and large language models.

That migration reflects the same market signal that is driving Cognition's thesis — experienced practitioners in the security space believe AI security is at an early-stage inflection point that resembles the formative periods of endpoint detection and cloud security, categories that produced several of the sector's most valuable companies. The executives leaving established platforms to pursue early-stage investment or company formation are betting they can identify and back the category winners before the market consensus catches up.

For CrowdStrike, the pattern raises a question that extends beyond any individual departure: as AI security emerges as a distinct and rapidly expanding market segment, can established platform players maintain their competitive position against purpose-built startups, or will the platform-reset moment that Cognition is betting on require incumbents to rebuild significant portions of their product architecture to remain relevant?

A $1,000 investment in CrowdStrike five years ago would be worth approximately $3,262 today — a measure of the value created under the leadership team that is now beginning to transition. Whether the next five years produce comparable returns will depend significantly on how the company navigates both the AI opportunity and the succession question that Thursday's news has brought into focus.

Sources

CrowdStrike Holdings share price data, Thursday August 2026. Elia Zaitsev interview on Cognition fund launch, August 2026. Gur Talpaz and Tayler Sipperly statements on Cognition investment thesis and SGNL exit track record, August 2026. Frost & Sullivan 2026 Frost Radar Cloud Workload Protection Platforms report, August 2026. CrowdStrike fiscal 2027 Q2 earnings date, August 26, 2026.

data.title: Elon Musk’s X Could Use USDC To Pay Global Creators As It Replaces Its Existing Revenue Sharing Model
data.description:
X Explores USDC Payments For Creators As It Reworks Revenue Sharing

X is exploring whether stablecoins such as Circle’s USDC could be used to pay influencers and content creators, as Elon Musk’s social media platform prepares to replace its existing creator revenue-sharing system.

The discussions are still ongoing and have not resulted in a confirmed payment plan, according to people familiar with the matter.

X has not officially announced USDC or any other stablecoin as a payout option.

🚨ELON MUSK’S X EXPLORES STABLECOINS TO PAY CREATORS!@elonmusk’s X is in talks to use stablecoins like Circle’s USDC to pay royalties to influencers and content providers for their uploads, according to @CoinDesk.

The discussions are ongoing, per a person familiar with the… pic.twitter.com/6uz6ym4NJk

— Crypto Banter (@crypto_banter) August 20, 2026

X Looks To Stablecoins For Global Creator Payments

The talks centre on the use of dollar-pegged stablecoins, with USDC among the options being considered.

Other stablecoins could also be part of the discussions.

For X, stablecoin payments could offer a simpler way to send dollar-denominated rewards to creators in different countries.

Unlike traditional international transfers, stablecoin transactions can move across borders without relying entirely on conventional banking networks, potentially reducing delays and payment costs.

The discussions are not limited to X.

The people familiar with the matter said other social media companies are also testing stablecoins as a way to pay creators and influencers.

Stablecoins have grown into a major part of the crypto market, with their combined market value surpassing $300 billion.

Their use for payments has also increased as companies look for faster ways to move money across borders.

Why Is X Changing Its Creator Payment System?

The potential stablecoin plan comes as X moves away from its existing Creator Revenue Sharing programme.

X stopped accepting new applications for the programme on 7 August, with the existing system scheduled to be retired on 7 September.

It is being replaced by the Original Content Rewards Programme, which places greater emphasis on original reporting, analysis, creativity and commentary.

JUST IN: X to end current creator monetization program and replace it with new "Original Content Rewards Program."

All existing creators will have to re-apply starting September 8th. pic.twitter.com/8FYbKCv7t7

— Watcher.Guru (@WatcherGuru) August 7, 2026

Under the new programme, X currently uses a payment processor to handle creator rewards.

The company has not said that stablecoins will be used, meaning any USDC-based payout system remains a possible future addition rather than a confirmed feature.

The timing of the discussions is therefore closely linked to X's broader overhaul of how creators are paid and rewarded on the platform.

Musk’s Other Businesses Already Use Stablecoins

Musk's interest in crypto payments extends beyond X.

SpaceX uses stablecoins to collect international payments from Starlink customers, particularly in markets where traditional payment systems can be less convenient.

That experience could provide a foundation for considering a similar approach for X's global creator network.

X is also developing its own payments infrastructure through X Money, as Musk continues to pursue his long-standing goal of turning the platform into a broader financial and communications service.

Meet the 𝕏 Card

› Up to 3% cashback on eligible purchases
› Free ATM withdrawals globally
› No foreign transaction fees pic.twitter.com/LZrlMs1D15

— X Money (@XMoney) August 10, 2026

The company has also brought in executives with crypto industry experience.

In March, X hired Benji Taylor, a former design lead at Coinbase's Base blockchain platform, as head of design across X, xAI and SpaceX.

Taylor's appointment gives the wider group additional experience in areas including crypto wallets and decentralised finance, although there is no confirmation that his hiring is directly connected to the stablecoin discussions.

USDC Could Give X A Global Dollar Payment Rail

For creators earning money from an international audience, receiving dollar-denominated stablecoins could provide an alternative to conventional bank transfers.

USDC is designed to maintain a value of $1, allowing payments to be made in a digital asset while avoiding the price swings associated with cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ether.

For X, the approach could also fit with its wider plans to combine social media, commerce and financial services within one platform.

However, the company has yet to confirm whether USDC will become part of its creator payment system, and there is no announced launch date.

Until X provides further details, creators should not assume that rewards under the Original Content Rewards Programme will be paid in stablecoins.

data.title: AirTag Hidden In Rare Book Leads To Amazon Facility Where Books Are Reportedly Destroyed For AI
data.description:
A $29 Apple AirTag hidden inside a used book has led journalists to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas, where books reportedly destined for AI training are stripped of their bindings, scanned and discarded.

The discovery by 404 Media provides one of the clearest public accounts yet of where large volumes of physical books bought through the second-hand market may be ending up.

An AirTag Tracked A Rare Book To Amazon’s Las Vegas Facility

404 Media worked with a bookseller to place an Apple AirTag inside a rare book included in a bulk shipment of roughly 1,000 volumes.

The tracker followed the shipment across four states before reaching an Amazon facility in northeast Las Vegas identified as LAS8.

Inside the site, the investigation linked the shipment to a team known as VGT3, which employees reportedly described as handling large shipments of printed books.

‼️ BREAKING: Journalists hid an Airtag in a rare book shipment and confirmed Amazon to be one of the buyers behind the bulk orders destroying rare-books to feed their AI.

They tracked it to Amazon's LAS8 warehouse in Las Vegas, home to VGT3 (see logo below), a scanning operation… pic.twitter.com/zOv4EkBHaE

— International Cyber Digest (@IntCyberDigest) August 17, 2026

Workers told 404 Media that books are processed by removing their bindings so the pages can be fed through scanners more quickly.

The physical books are then discarded, leaving only the digitised text.

The VGT3 team even uses a logo showing a dinosaur holding a book in its claws, an unusual detail given the reported fate of the books passing through the operation.

Why Are Old Printed Books Valuable For AI Training?

The books are valuable because AI companies need vast amounts of high-quality text to train large language models.

Much of the easily accessible material on the internet has already been used for training, while older printed books can contain text that is difficult or impossible to find online.

Books published before 2022 are also attractive because their content is less likely to have been produced by AI systems.

AI companies are buying large volumes of used, rare, and out-of-print books, scanning them for training data, and in many cases destroying the physical copies afterward.

This practice has accelerated as labs seek high-quality, pre-2022 human-written text free of AI-generated… pic.twitter.com/fa8FwXH30a

— Massimo (@Rainmaker1973) July 31, 2026

Training models repeatedly on AI-generated material can contribute to "model collapse", a problem where the quality and diversity of model outputs can deteriorate over successive training cycles.

That has created a new demand for older, human-written material, including out-of-print and rare books.

Amazon Says It Buys Books Through Commercial Channels

Amazon did not confirm the specific findings of the 404 Media investigation.

Instead, the company said:

"Amazon purchases books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services our customers use."

The statement does not explain how the books are processed after purchase or whether material from the scanned books is used specifically to train Amazon’s AI models.

The investigation is particularly notable because Amazon had previously faced allegations over destructive book scanning.

The AirTag tracking provides physical evidence of at least one bulk shipment reaching an Amazon site associated with book scanning, although it does not by itself establish that every book purchased through the same channels is being used for AI training.

The AirTag investigation links one shipment to an Amazon facility where employees reportedly described destructive scanning

It does not by itself establish the scale of the operation or which specific Amazon models received the data

— Sam Tilston (@samtilston) August 17, 2026

Booksellers Have Seen A Surge In Unusual Bulk Orders

The demand has also created a new business for booksellers dealing in used and unwanted titles.

Some sellers have reported receiving unusually large orders containing books that other buyers would normally ignore.

The buyers also appeared less concerned about price than conventional customers, with some orders involving substantial shipping costs because of the number of books involved.

One bookseller cited in the reporting described a case where a book sold for €5 incurred €40 in shipping costs, while the overall business generated a medium five-figure sum.

I'm a second-generation bookseller. My family runs Houston's largest used & rare bookstore and I'm building an AI tool for used bookstores. We got hit by exactly these orders, including a single order for 70 obscure books that made us pause online sales entirely. So I dug in. I… https://t.co/IK7OE8f1DG

— Charlie D. Becker (@charliedbecker) July 28, 2026

For sellers, the orders can provide an important source of income for books that might otherwise remain unsold.

But the practice has also raised concerns about rare and historically valuable books being destroyed after their contents are digitised.

The Legal Battle Over Books And AI Training Is Growing

The use of books for AI training has already become a major legal issue.

Anthropic faced a lawsuit over its use of books, with a US federal judge ruling that training AI on legally purchased books can qualify as fair use.

Meta and OpenAI have also relied on similar arguments in legal disputes over copyrighted material.

The situation is different when books are obtained illegally.

Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion settlement over claims involving scanned pirated books, while Salesforce faces a class action lawsuit alleging book piracy linked to AI training.

A federal judge today approved the largest copyright class settlement in U.S. history. $1.5 billion from Anthropic to authors who said their books were used as training data for Claude. Preliminary approval came last September. https://t.co/9xU6yUJOeKpic.twitter.com/JQD1AHUCVp

— Andrew Curran (@AndrewCurran_) July 20, 2026

The legal distinction between lawfully purchased books and pirated copies has therefore become central to the debate over how AI companies obtain training data.

Anthropic Has Already Used Destructive Scanning At Scale

Amazon is not the only company linked to the practice.

Anthropic’s internal "Project Panama" reportedly involved the destructive scanning of millions of books, turning physical copies into digital training material.

That has helped create a wider supply chain in which books are purchased, transported to scanning facilities, stripped of their bindings and ultimately discarded.

THIS IS F*CKING DISTURBING!!!🤯

A leaked Anthropic document just came out in court. Their own words:

"Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world."

Next line: "We don't want it to be known that we are working on this."

They planned to shred… pic.twitter.com/qKjDPxevX0

— Evan Luthra (@EvanLuthra) July 29, 2026

The 404 Media investigation adds a physical location to a practice that has largely remained hidden from public view.

For rare books, the concern is not simply that a copy is being digitised.

Once the binding is removed and the physical pages are discarded, that particular copy may be gone permanently.

data.title: Why Voluntary Age Checks on AI Chatbots Are Not Enough to Protect Children
data.description:
Why Voluntary Age Checks on AI Chatbots Are Not Enough to Protect Children

OpenAI's launch of a dedicated ChatGPT experience for teenagers is a step in the right direction. But it exposes a fundamental problem with how the AI industry is approaching youth safety: if age verification is voluntary, optional and never independently confirmed, the safeguards designed to protect minors will only reach the children whose parents or guardians ensure they are using the right account. Every other child remains unprotected.

Key Points

  • ChatGPT for Teens, rolled out from August 19, filters content promoting self-harm, violence, eating disorders, dangerous activities and explicit sex — but relies on voluntary self-declaration of age
  • Users detected by OpenAI's system to be under 18 are automatically classified as teen accounts, but detection is imperfect and self-declaration can be bypassed
  • Several suicides have been linked to AI chatbots, including the 2024 death of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer III, who became obsessed with a character on Character.AI
  • Singapore's IMDA has required app stores to prevent under-18 users from downloading inappropriate apps since April, using government ID, credit card data, facial scanning and usage pattern analysis
  • Academics and regulators are calling for mandatory age verification to be extended to AI chatbots
  • Without consistent age verification across platforms, minors will migrate to whichever chatbot has the fewest restrictions

What ChatGPT for Teens Does — And What It Doesn't

OpenAI's teen-specific ChatGPT experience applies content filters designed to block material that promotes self-harm, violence, eating disorders, dangerous activities and sexually explicit content. Users under 18 are prompted to declare their age during account registration, and accounts that OpenAI's systems independently detect as likely belonging to a minor are automatically classified as teen accounts.

The intent is sound. The implementation has a structural weakness: it relies on a voluntary declaration that can be bypassed by any minor who provides an incorrect age at registration. There is no independent verification mechanism that confirms whether the age entered during account creation is accurate. A 14-year-old who wants access to the unrestricted version of ChatGPT can create an account claiming to be 20 without any technical barrier preventing it.

The automatic detection system provides a partial backstop — OpenAI's platform can infer age from behavioural signals even when incorrect information is provided — but detection is imperfect by design. It catches some underage users who misrepresent their age. It does not catch all of them. And those it misses are precisely the users the safeguards were designed to protect.

The Harms That Made This Necessary

The urgency behind youth AI safety measures is not hypothetical. Since generative AI chatbots entered mainstream use in 2022, a growing body of documented harm has demonstrated what happens when children interact with AI systems designed primarily for adults.

The most severe cases involve fatalities. In 2024, 14-year-old Sewell Setzer III died by suicide after developing an intense attachment to a character he had created on Character.AI. His mother filed a lawsuit in Florida against the company, accusing it of building a product that targeted her son with anthropomorphic, hypersexualised and frighteningly realistic experiences that ultimately led him to prefer the fictional world the chatbot had created over his own life. The case resulted in a settlement and prompted significant regulatory and public attention to the question of how AI platforms should handle interactions with minors.

Other documented harms include AI chatbots exhibiting sycophantic behaviour that reinforces negative beliefs in vulnerable users, providing explicit advice about methods of self-harm, and — in the case of xAI's Grok earlier this year — generating non-consensual sexual content involving real people en masse on X before restrictions were implemented. The pattern across these incidents is consistent: AI systems designed without adequate youth protections cause specific and serious harm to minors when accessed without restriction.

The Limits of Platform Self-Regulation

The current approach — in which AI platforms implement youth safety measures voluntarily, define their own standards and rely on self-declaration for age verification — has produced uneven results. Some platforms have introduced meaningful safeguards. Others have moved only under regulatory or public pressure after harm has already occurred. The Grok image generation incident and the Character.AI lawsuit both illustrate that voluntary measures, implemented at the platform's discretion and on the platform's timeline, are insufficient when the users most at risk cannot be relied upon to navigate opt-in safety systems correctly.

The deeper structural problem, identified by researchers and policymakers, is one of migration. Without consistent age verification requirements across AI platforms, minors who are blocked from accessing unrestricted content on one platform will simply move to another that has fewer restrictions. A robust safety framework on one chatbot provides no protection if the next chatbot in a browser search has none. The protection is only as strong as the least restricted platform in the ecosystem.

"Without a consistent way of implementing age checks, users will simply migrate to chatbots with the least restrictions and the whole effort to protect minors risks being defeated," said Lim Sun Sun, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Communication and Technology at Singapore Management University.

Singapore's Regulatory Model

Singapore has moved further than most jurisdictions toward mandatory age verification for digital services. Since April 2026, the Infocomm Media Development Authority has required app stores to prevent Singapore users under 18 from downloading inappropriate applications — including those providing dating services or containing sexual content. The verification methods available include checking government-issued identity documents, credit card information, facial scanning and analysis of online usage patterns.

Plans are in place to extend mandatory age verification to social media services, with particular concern focused on unmanaged direct messaging from strangers and automatic video playback features — categories that overlap significantly with how AI chatbots are increasingly being embedded within social media and messaging platforms. As those lines blur, the regulatory framework will need to expand to cover AI interfaces that operate within the same ecosystems as direct messaging and content feeds.

Lim argued that the regulatory intervention Singapore has applied to app stores and social media should extend to all emerging technology that young people access, including AI chatbots. "This would go towards securing greater ownership by AI companies in their responsibility towards younger users," she said.

What Mandatory Age Verification Would Require

Implementing effective mandatory age verification for AI chatbots presents genuine technical and policy challenges. Age verification methods that rely on government ID or credit card data exclude minors who are the intended beneficiaries of the protection — the verification design must distinguish between a 17-year-old who should be restricted and a 17-year-old who is the parent or guardian creating an account on behalf of their family.

Behavioural and biometric verification approaches — facial scanning and usage pattern analysis — introduce their own privacy considerations, particularly for minors whose data would be collected as part of the verification process. Any mandatory framework must balance the protection benefit against the data protection implications of the verification mechanism itself.

What the Singapore model demonstrates is that these challenges are solvable. Governments that choose to treat age verification as a regulatory requirement rather than a platform discretion have the tools to implement it. What has been lacking in most jurisdictions is the political will to require it of AI platforms that have resisted external oversight as vigorously as they have resisted restrictions on model capability development.

The Case for Action

The argument for mandatory age verification on AI chatbots rests on a straightforward premise: voluntary measures that can be bypassed by the users they are designed to protect are not adequate protection. ChatGPT for Teens is a better product for young users than unrestricted ChatGPT. But it only reaches the minors who access it through a verified teen account — and it currently has no reliable mechanism for ensuring that every minor who uses ChatGPT is accessing it that way.

The harms that have already occurred — including deaths — were not prevented by the voluntary safeguards that existed at the time. Waiting for more harm to accumulate before requiring platforms to verify the age of their users is a policy choice that treats children's safety as less urgent than AI companies' operational preferences.

As AI chatbots become more deeply embedded in how young people learn, communicate and process their experiences, the question of who is responsible for ensuring they are not harmed in that process becomes more consequential, not less. The technology companies that build these systems have demonstrated they will move at their own pace on safety unless they are required to move faster.

Sources

The Straits Times reporting on ChatGPT for Teens launch, August 19, 2026. OpenAI ChatGPT for Teens feature announcement, August 2026. Sewell Setzer III Character.AI lawsuit and settlement, 2024–2025. xAI Grok non-consensual image generation incident, January 2026. Singapore IMDA mandatory age verification for app stores, April 2026. Lim Sun Sun, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Communication and Technology, Singapore Management University, statement on regulatory intervention, 2026. The Straits Times opinion piece on mandatory AI chatbot age checks, August 2026.
